en: We shall explain the applications for laying out the sacrificial altars according to the *Āpastamba-Śulbasūtra*.
The measurement is according to its length. ĀpŚus 1.2a.
Having practiced that half-measure on the other [side], he makes the mark on the third [side] when it is reduced by one-sixth.
Having fixed the two ends at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line by means of a mark, he draws it southward and makes a mark.
In this way, having reversed [the sequence] from the north, that concentration is [performed] in the opposite direction. ĀpŚus 1.2d.
The decrease or increase is caused by that [measure]. ĀpŚus 1.2e.
Having practiced the length (āyāma) as the fourth [side], the length is the diagonal cord (akṣṇayā rajju), and the remainder is the cross-measure (tiryaṅbhānī).
The method of laying out (viharaṇa) has been explained. ĀpŚus 1.3a.
The diagonal cord of the long [altar] performs both that which the side-measuring cord and the crosswise-measuring cord perform when they are separate. ĀpŚus_1.4a //
The dwelling has been described by those [verses] which are to be known.
The diagonal cord of a square produces an area twice as large;
it is the multiplier for doubling when [the sides] are equalized. (ĀpŚus 1.5)
One should increase the measurement by one-third; that [increase] is with distinction by means of the fourth, which is less than thirty-four parts of itself. ĀpŚus 1.6.
Now, another [rite]. ĀpŚus_1.7a.
He makes a rope of the exact length, with loops at both ends.
Having stretched the *pṛṣṭhyā* cord from the mark in the middle to the marks at the two halves, he drives stakes into the marks at the two ends;
then, having fastened the two loops onto the two penultimate stakes, he pulls [the cord] southward by means of the central mark and makes a stake as a marker.
Then, having fastened the two loops onto the central [stake],...
One should stretch [the cord] over the right shoulder from above using the middle mark;
having released it from the front and fastened it at the back, one should stretch it over the right hip using the same middle mark.
In the same way for the left hip and shoulder. (ĀpŚus 1.7c)
Now follows another method. ĀpŚus_2.1a.
Having driven stakes at the two ends of the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and in its middle, and having added half of that interval to each half and made a mark, one should bring the cord to the midpoint.
Having made loops at the two ends and fastening the cord with the extra length on the middle stake, one should draw the southern shoulder from the front stake using the other [end] and the mark.
Having unfastened it from the front stake and fastened it on the back stake, one should likewise draw the southern hip using the mark.
In the same way, [he places] the two northern hips and shoulders. ĀpŚus_2.1b.
The measurement across is two karaṇīs; its length is three karaṇīs, which serves as the diagonal cord. (ĀpŚS 2.2)
The third *karaṇī* is explained by this [same method];
however, its division is ninefold. (ĀpŚS 2.3)
The combination of two equal squares has been explained; now follows the combination of two squares of different dimensions. ĀpŚus 2.4a.
One should mark the larger [post] from the corner of the smaller one;
the cord stretched diagonally across the larger [post] brings both together.
This has been explained. (ĀpŚus_2.4b)
If one wishes to extract a square from a square, one should draw a diagonal line across the larger [square] over as much of it as one intends to extract.
One should extend the cord along the side of the wider [side] and bring it to meet the other side diagonally.
Wherever that [blade] should fall, one should cut off that portion. ĀpŚus_2.5c.
It is cast away with the *chinnayā* [formula]. (ĀpŚus_2.5d)
The cord, having its unpropitious parts removed and divided into four parts, performs both that which the other two cords, when separate, perform individually.
The horizontal measuring-line [measures] one man; the remainder [measures] three.
Thus it has been said: ĀpŚus_2.6d.
One desiring to make a long quadrangle into a square should cut off a portion along the cross-measure, divide the remainder, and lay it down on both sides.
One should fill up any breakage with something brought from elsewhere. ĀpŚus_2.7b.
Its performance has been explained. ĀpŚus_2.7c.
One who wishes to make [a fire-altar] a perfect square or a long rectangle should make the side-measure as large as he desires; whatever remains in excess, he should place it accordingly. (ĀpŚS 3.1)
One desiring to make a square mandala should drop [the cord] from the center to the corner. (ĀpŚus 3.2a)
Having drawn [the cord] along the side, one should trace the mandala together with an additional third part.
That [altar] is eternal; it is the maṇḍala. ĀpŚus_3.2c.
As long as it is held, so long does it come. ĀpŚus_3.2d.
Desiring to construct a square mandala, one should divide the diameter into fifteen parts and set aside two;
thirteen remain. That is the constant square. (ĀpŚus 3.3)
The measurement is prescribed by means of a measuring instrument.
Anything other than a square is [formed] by command. ĀpŚus_3.5.
By means of two [verses], four [libations]. ĀpŚus_3.6a.
With three [verses], nine [stomas]. ĀpŚus 3.6b.
As many times as the cord is measured, that many squares he makes.
Three and a half men [in height] for six [bricks], each with a quarter-part added.
Now follows the rule for the extreme limit. Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.9a.
To whatever extent he draws around with an excess [of material], he places that on the two sides;
and that which is made square by him, he places at the corner. (ĀpŚus 3.9b)
The measurement of the foot is prescribed as half the measurement [of the body].
Because the half [verse] consists of two measures for the purpose of completing the line. (ĀpŚus 3.10b)
By the third [offering], the ninth part is completed. ĀpŚus_3.10c.
In the sacrificial enclosure for the establishment of the fires (āgnīdheya), it is known that [the path] lies between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires. (ĀpŚus 4.1a)
A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fire at eight steps;
a Rājanya at eleven;
a Vaiśya at twelve. (ĀpŚus 4.1b)

It is heard in all [the Śrautasūtras] without distinction that [the fire] should be placed at a distance not too far from where one perceives it with the eye, whether that be twenty-four [finger-breadths], immeasurable, or as much as one can judge by sight. (ĀpŚus 4.2)
It is known from the *Āpastamba Śulbasūtra* 4.3 that [the location] for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is at the third part from the south-east, closer to the Gārhapatya fire.
Having divided the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires into five or six parts, and having added a sixth or seventh part as an addition,
he divides it equally into three. Having made a mark on the third part from the end,
and having fixed the two ends at the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya, he draws a line toward the south along the mark and makes a reference-point there.
The location for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire [is established] by the force of the Vedic revelation. (ĀpŚus 4.4)
The eastern side of the altar is equal to the height of the sacrificer, or it may be unlimited; the crosswise side is made so that the sacrificial oblations may fit upon it.

He raises the two shoulders of the altar toward the east; the two hips are turned westward; it is narrower in front and broader behind, being more deeply curved in the middle—for thus is a woman—so it is known from the altar used for the New Moon sacrifice. (ĀpŚus_4.5)

To the west of the Āhavanīya fire, having marked out a long square measuring one fathom on each side for the sacrificer, he stretches a cord of that same length, makes a mark in the middle, and fixing it between the two southern corners (the left hip and the right shoulder), he pulls it toward the south along the mark and makes a reference point.
Having fixed the cord at that reference point and brought the two ends together, he folds them in half.
From the southern hip, one should draw a line to the southern shoulder;
likewise from the northern side. Having thus made the cross-measure double, one should then draw lines both backwards and forwards.
In the case of a square [altar], one should contract the two lateral sides at the front, by virtue of the force of the scriptural injunction. (Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra 4.6)
It is known from the *Saumikī-vedi* that it is thirty paces or steps wide from west to east, thirty-six paces long from south to north, and twenty-four paces wide from east to west. (ĀpŚus 5.1)

In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśikā*, having combined eighteen [units], one fixes the two ends of the spine at the other two ends; having extended twelve units from the end of the spine, one drives in a peg; likewise on the north side for the two hips.
Having reversed the procedure, having extended fifteen units [from the center] toward the shoulders, one drives in a peg at the twelve-unit mark.
In this same manner, the two shoulders are [placed] toward the north.
The measuring out [of the altar] is performed with a single cord.
The diagonal cord for the two [sets of] three and four [units] is fivefold.
With those [cords] repeated three times, the shoulders are formed; with them repeated four times, the hips. (ĀpŚS 5.3)

The diagonal cord for the twelve-and-five [fathom] and thirteen-and-five [fathom] altars is thirteen [fathoms]; with those doubled, the two shoulders are formed; with them [the same], the two hips are formed. (ĀpŚus 5.4)
The diagonal cord for the fifteen-unit and eight-unit [sides] is the seventeen-unit cord; with these, the two hips [are measured]. (ĀpŚus 5.5a)
The diagonal cord for the twelve-fingered and thirty-five-fingered [boards] is the thirty-seven-fingered one; with these, the two shoulders [are marked]. (ĀpŚus 5.5b)
There are this many altars and altar-sites to be known. // ĀpŚus_5.6 //
The great altar-ground measures one thousand minus twenty-eight paces.
From the right shoulder, one should lay down [the bricks] in twelve places ending at the right hip;
having reversed the cutting, one should place them from the north.
That is a long quadrangle.
He should look at her when she is positioned in that manner. ĀpŚus_5.7b.
"One should sacrifice in the third part of the Vedic altar of the Soma sacrifice"—this is known from the Sautrāmaṇī regarding the altar.
The side of this [altar] is either twice the measure of a *prakrama* or equal to three *prakramas*. ĀpŚus_5.8b //
The *aṣṭikā* and the *daśikā* are the transverse measures;
the *dvādaśikā* is the *pṛṣṭhyā*.
The Sautrāmaṇī altar measures three hundred and twenty-four padas. ĀpŚus 5.9.
"It is known in the Aśvamedha that the altar is twice as large [as the usual size]. (ĀpŚus 5.10)
The double-measure of the step becomes equivalent to the position of the step itself.
The step consists of two or three feet.
Regarding the step, one may act as desired, because the meaning of the word is subject to such variation. (ĀpŚS 6.2a)
It belongs either to the sacrificer or to the Adhvaryu priest;
for he is the performer of the ritual actions. (ĀpŚus_6.2b)
It is known from tradition that the sacrificial altar for one who has performed the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice is the size of a chariot.
Its axle was indeed as long as a chariot-axle; it was oriented westward across the pole and eastward across the yoke-pins. ĀpŚus_6.3b //
Or as far as there is a hole on the outside. ĀpŚus_6.3c.
This has been stated by means of a single cord:
"With a fifteen-fold cord, using half an axle and half a yoke, one should determine the hips and shoulders. (ĀpŚS 6.4)
Moreover, they also cite this: ĀpŚus_6.5a.
The pole is one hundred and eighty-eight [units] across, the axle four hundred, and its yoke eighty-six; this is called the moving chariot—such is the measurement of the chariot. (ĀpŚus 6.5b)
Alternatively, with four cubits at the back, six at the east, and three at the front;
that which was described as being with a single cord—having pulled it out by fifteen [units] using two and one-and-a-half [units] respectively—one should mark off the hips and shoulders. (ĀpŚus 6.6)
"It is known from the ritual manual for the ancestral altar (paitṛkī vedi) that it should be four-cornered and equal in measure to the sacrificer;
this is described by means of a single cord using a fifteen-fold [measure]. Having laid it out by half [of that length], one should then mark off the two corners and the two shoulders. (ĀpŚus 6.7)
"It is known from the Soma ritual that the altar is ten paces wide.
This is stated by means of a single cord; having measured it with a fifteen-fold [cord], one should then mark out the two hips and the two shoulders from that [central point]. (ĀpŚus 6.8)
Having measured that [altar] with a yoke or by the steps of the sacrificer, he measures it around with a wooden pin (śamyā).

In the case of the words *pada*, *yuga*, *aratni*, *iyati*, and *śamyā*, when used for the purpose of measurement, one may use them according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is subject to variation.
In the case of a square [altar], one should bring together the side-measures at the front, by virtue of the force of the scriptural injunction. (ĀpŚus 6.11)
It is known that the Sadas measures nine aratnis across and twenty-seven [aratnis] in length toward the north. ĀpŚus 7.1.
According to some, there are eighteen [officiating priests]. (ĀpŚus 7.2)
Having stated that with a single cord, one should mark out the hips and shoulders using fifteen [units] and four and a half [units] respectively. ĀpŚus 7.3.
It is known from scripture that the *uparavas* have openings of one span (*prādeśa*) and intervals between them of one span.

Having marked out a square measuring one cubit (*aratni*), one should drive stakes into its corners and, by the force of the scriptural injunction, trace each [corner] with a radius of half a span. (ĀpŚS 7.4)
"It becomes the measure of physical exertion," so it is understood from the Gārhapatya altar. (ĀpŚus_7.5)
According to some, it is square; according to others, it is circular. ĀpŚS 7.6.
One should cause the third stride of the *vyāyāma* to be seven *vyāmas* in width. ĀpŚus 7.7.
These become twenty-one. ĀpŚus_7.8 //
In the first layer they run eastward; in the other [layer], they run northward.
Having formed a mound of earth in the center of the mandala and having fixed a peg (śaṅku) in its middle, one should draw the circle with a cord equal to half the diameter. ĀpŚus_7.10a //
One should fix a square upon that as far as it may extend; having marked it out in nine parts, one should divide each part further into three. (ĀpŚus 7.10b)
In the setting of the bricks for the square altar, one should form the corners toward the intermediate directions.
In the other arrangement, it is brought in at the middle. // ĀpŚus_7.11b //
One should pile them in alternating fashion for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
"It is known from the ritual tradition that the hearths (dhiṣṇyas) are merely a span in size. (ĀpŚus_7.12)
According to some, they are square; according to others, they are circular. ĀpŚus 7.13.
Having made earthen images and having drawn nine lines across the Āgnīdhrīya altar, one should place a stone in the position of one of them. ĀpŚus 7.14.
Having drawn the other [lines] in their respective order, one should place them accordingly as appropriate. (ĀpŚus 7.15)
"It is indeed known: 'He who piles the fire-altar becomes, as it were, [a bird]'";
for it is enjoined by way of its form that "this [altar] is piled in the likeness of birds," or because of the direct injunction [of its shape]. (ĀpŚus 8.1)
With a bamboo measuring rod as long as the traditional measurement, he measures out the Puruṣas within the square self. (ĀpŚus 8.2a)
A man on the right wing, a man on the tail, and a man on the left.
He extends the right wing by one cubit on the south; likewise, he extends the left wing on the north. ĀpŚus 8.2c.
The tail is [measured] by one span or by a palm behind.
The first fire is of one kind, the second is of two kinds, and the third is of three kinds; these indeed emerge in this very manner from the one hundred and one-fold fire.
One should indeed pile it as having seven forms;
for the original fire-altar is indeed sevenfold.
It is known from scripture that beyond that, the layers increase by one each. (ĀpŚus 8.4)

For those [altars] consisting of one kind and so forth, there are no wings or tails, because of the remainder of the statement regarding the seven kinds and because of a contradiction with the revealed scripture (śruti). (ĀpŚus 8.5)
Of those [offerings] beginning with eightfold, whatever remains after the sevenfold ones, one should divide that into seven parts and cause it to enter into each person.
Because no modification of the form is heard [in the scripture]. (ĀpŚus_8.6b)
"He measures with a man's length; he measures with a bamboo pole," so it is known. (ĀpŚus 8.7)
He makes an opening in the bamboo at a distance from one end equal to the height of the sacrificer with his arms raised; he makes the third opening in the middle. (ĀpŚus 8.8)

Another [assistant], having placed a bamboo pole along the spine at the location of the sacrificial post-hole, having driven stakes into its holes, and having released [the cord from the previous pegs], should trace around [the hole] toward the south-east with the other two [ends of the cord] until it reaches the edge.
Having unfastened it from the front and fastened it at the back, he should draw a line around it toward the south and west until the edge.

Having unfastened the bamboo at the middle peg and having fastened the last hole of the bamboo against it, he places the bamboo vertically above the line so that its end is level with the line; then, having driven a peg into the last hole, he fastens the middle hole of the bamboo against it, fixes the other two ends upon the two lines, and drives pegs into the two holes. (ĀpŚS 9.1a)
That man is square. ĀpŚus_9.1b.
In this manner, he measures out four persons within himself, from the front to the right.
A man on the right wing, a man at the tail, and a man on the left. (ĀpŚus 9.2b)
"It is said: 'With the cubit [measurement], from the south, the southern [side]'. (ĀpŚus_9.2c)
Or, having laid a bamboo measuring a man's height diagonally from the spine, with one end at the front and the other at the rear, one should mark out the southern shoulder from those two;
then, reversing them, [one marks] the two hips. (ĀpŚus 9.3a)
As before, [he places it] on the left shoulder. ĀpŚus_9.3b.
Or he measures it with a cord according to the method of the *uttaravedi*, or he measures it with a bamboo pole.

In the case of increasing or decreasing by one-third in the wings, tail, and flanks, one should perform the ritual after having made the *vidhāsaptama-karaṇī* (the side-measure corresponding to the seventh part) serve as the unit for the person. ĀpŚus 9.5.
One should cause the eight sacrificial implements to be made by a person who is the fifth [in lineage]. ĀpŚus_9.6a.
Of those very [bricks], one and a half [units] on one side constitute the second;
a fifth part of a man on one side and a span on the other constitutes the third. ĀpŚus 9.6b.
That which is a span on all sides is the fourth;
those which are equal squares of fifteen parts are the fifth.
The vertical measurement of the bricks should be made as five parts of the distance from one knee to the other.
With half [of that], [he worships] the Nākasads and the Pañcacūḍās.
Whatever part of the bricks being baked should sink down due to the filling material (purīṣa), that one should fill up again, because the quantity of the filling material is not fixed. (ĀpŚus 9.8)
In the foundation layer, he places ten bricks, one and a half units long, facing westward upon the body; ten facing eastward behind it. (ĀpŚus 10.1a)

There are five bricks at each of the two tips of the wings; at the two junctions of the wings, there are the objects of those [rows], measuring half a brick each, which belong to the two wings. ĀpŚus 10.1b.
Five by five [bricks] are placed on the two sides of the question, facing south and north.
Having placed a span-long brick at the tail, one should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks measuring five parts.
One should complete the count with fifteen-part shares. ĀpŚus 10.3.
In the next layer, he places ten bricks measuring one and a half [bricks] on the body, extending northwards on the south side, and ten extending southwards on the north side. (ĀpŚus 10.4a)
As the two wings are in the first layer, so are the tail;
as the tail is, so are the wings, though reversed at the point of convergence.
One should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks that have five parts.
One should complete the count with fifteen parts. (ĀpŚus 10.6a)
One should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers as one intends to construct.
There are five layers;
one covers them with five fillings. Thus, the layer ends with the filling, because the filling is a distinct entity. (ĀpŚus 10.7)
One building the fire-altar for the first time should pile it with a thousand bricks, knee-deep in height.
The second [altar] is two thousand [bricks], reaching up to the navel; the third is three thousand, reaching up to the mouth; each subsequent one is larger than the preceding. (ĀpŚus 10.8b)
"One who desires heaven should pile a great, vast, and immeasurable [altar]," so it is known.
In a two-thousand-fold [altar], there are altars with two layers;
in a three-thousand-fold [altar], there are altars with three layers; from the fourth offering onwards, the measurement of the bricks is constant. (ĀpŚS 10.9)
And it is known from scripture: "Having piled a larger altar, one should not pile a smaller one. (ĀpŚus 10.10)
"One should pile the fire-altar with squares," so it is known;
they are equal squares because the word has no qualifying adjunct. (ĀpŚus 11.1)
It is known from tradition that they are the size of a foot, the size of a cubit, the size of a thigh-bone, and the size of a small bone. ĀpŚus 11.2.
A four-part measure is a maṇūka; a five-part measure is an aratni; likewise is an ūrvasthi. ĀpŚus 11.3a.
A brick for the foot is one-quarter of a measure.
In that case, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is intended to apply to the object.
On the two shoulder-projections (upadhāna), one should place eight four-part bricks (caturbhāgīyā) on each wing-tip;
and likewise at the two joints (sandhi), [one should place them] leaving a space of six finger-breadths from the body (ātman).
And eight [lines] on the hips and shoulders, running both eastward and westward.
In the interval between the *sandhi*s, there are five parts plus one-quarter. ĀpŚus 11.6.
Having placed a span-long brick at the tail, one should cover the entire fire-altar with four-part bricks.
One should complete the count with brick-pieces for the feet. (ĀpŚus 11.8)
In the subsequent layout, at the junction of the tail, there are five-part bricks extending across.
One should place those [bricks] upon the self with fourteen feet, as appropriate. ĀpŚus 11.9b.
One should cover the entire fire-altar with bricks that constitute the fifth part.
One should complete the count with bricks for the feet. ĀpŚus_11.11a.
One should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
One should have the bricks made in the proportions of twelve and thirteen for the sacrificial measures (karaṇīs) starting from the single-fold and so forth. ĀpŚus 12.1a.
And one should lay down the foot-bricks alternately for as many layers as one intends to construct.

For those [altars] consisting of one kind and so forth, the measurement for the first, second, and third [altars] should be joined respectively with the first, second, and third measures; for all of them, the upward measurement is according to the numerical order as heard in the scripture. ĀpŚus 12.2.
The optional rites are modifications of the constituent qualities, because they are taught as being based on those qualities.
"One who has rivals should pile the prauga-citi," so it is known.

Having made a square plot of ground twice as large as the fire-altar measuring one *aratni* and one *prādeśa*, one should draw the two hips from the midpoint of the eastern side toward the [western] end; that is the permanent *prauga* altar. (ĀpŚus 12.5)
The ritual acts consist of piling; thus it is stated to be of one kind. (ĀpŚus 12.6a)
One should have the *prauga* bricks made.
"One who desires, 'May I drive away my born enemies and those yet to be born,' should pile the Prauga altar in both ways; so it is known. (ĀpŚus 12.7)
Just as when a cart has its face turned away. ĀpŚus 12.8.

Having laid out the altar as square as it is long, one should mark off from the midpoint of the eastern and western sides a distance equal to that [side], and drop marks on the southern and northern sides; that is the perpetual *prauga* (fore-part) on both sides. (ĀpŚS 12.9)
Regarding the statements on the *prauga-cit*:
one should have bricks made that are shaped like a *prauga* on both sides. (Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra 12.10)
"One who has rivals should pile it in the form of a chariot wheel," so it is known.
Having made a circular area of ground as large as the fire-altar together with the *aratni* and *prādeśa* measures, one should place a square [altar] upon it as far as it can fit. (ĀpŚus 12.12)
One should have twelve bricks made from its [the altar's] span.
Having placed six of them upon the foundation stone, one should divide the remainder into eight parts.
In the layering of the square altar, one should form the corners toward the intermediate directions; in the other layer, one should place the middle bricks.
One should pile them in an alternating manner for as many layers as one intends to construct. (ĀpŚus 13.3)
"One should pile the Droṇacit for one who desires food," so it is known from tradition.
There are indeed two types [of measures]:
square and circular. ĀpŚus 13.5.
In that case, one may act according to one's desire, because the meaning of the word is intended to apply to all objects.
Or it may be square for one whose treatise on qualities [is such].
And it is square. ĀpŚus_13.8.
"It subsequently becomes a handle because of its suitability," so it is understood.
The tenth part of the entire ground is the handle; its removal by means of the tail has been described.
One should have twelve bricks made from that [measure], as well as one-and-a-half-sized bricks and quarter-bricks. (ĀpŚus 13.11)
On the *upadhāna* layer, he places one and a half bricks on the front part facing west upon himself, and on the two hips facing east in the *tsaru*-section. (ĀpŚS 13.12)
One should cover the entire fire-altar with square bricks.
One should complete the count with brick-pieces for the base. (Āpastamba Śulba Sūtra 13.14)

In the next layer, he places bricks measuring one and a half [bricks] on the self (ātman), extending northwards from the south and southwards from the north; on the two sides of the handle, he places those extending southwards and northwards. 13.15.
One should cover the entire fire-altar with square bricks.
One should complete the count with bricks for the feet. ĀpŚus_13.17.
One should pile them in reverse order for as many layers (prastāra) as one intends to construct.
"One who desires cattle should pile the *samūhya*," so it is known.
He piles the bricks while indeed removing [the previous layer]. ĀpŚus_14.2.
The sacrificial pits (cātvālas) are located in the cardinal directions; it is known from scripture that one draws out the earth from them toward the east. (ĀpŚus 14.3)
"One who desires a village should pile the Paricāyya fire-altar," so it is known.
He encloses the central naturally perforated brick with groups of bricks moving clockwise;
that is the *pariyāyya*. (ĀpŚus 14.5)

The length of the wings is nine and a half cubits minus one-fourth of an angula.
